title: Ah Ma's Ngoh Hiang and the CNY Tradition That Brings Us Home
excerpt: It is not the dish that makes it special. It is the hands that make it together.
content:
Every Chinese New Year, without fail, my family gathers at my ah ma's place for one thing: to make ngoh hiang together.

Not to eat it (though that part comes later, and it is glorious). But to stand around her kitchen counter, sleeves rolled up, getting our hands dirty together, doing something that none of us would bother doing alone.

It has been this way for as long as I can remember.

For those who have not come across it before, ngoh hiang (五香) is a traditional Chinese dish, sometimes called "five spice roll." At its core, it is seasoned minced meat wrapped in thin beancurd skin, then fried until golden and crispy on the outside, savoury and tender within. It is one of those dishes that almost every Chinese household knows. And almost every household makes it a little differently.

My ah ma's version has a few things that make it distinctly hers. Water chestnuts, for the crunch. Mushrooms and prawns, for depth and texture. And carrots, for a gentle sweetness that rounds everything out.

The preparation itself is actually really straightforward, which is part of why it works so well as a family activity. It starts with the chopping. Mushrooms, water chestnuts, carrots, prawns, all diced up until the cutting board is just a mess of colour. Then everything gets thrown into these big metal bowls with the minced pork, seasoned, and mixed together by hand until it all comes together.

Next comes the beancurd skins. They come dried, and the surface is covered with these tiny salt crystals. So before wrapping, every sheet needs to be wiped down with a damp cloth to get rid of the excess salt.

After that, it is just wrapping. Scoop the filling onto a sheet of beancurd skin. Fold, tuck, roll. Repeat. Chatting, laughing, hands moving.

Some traditions are not preserved through documentation. They are preserved through showing up.

title: The Death of the Hackathon Spirit: Startups, Pre-baking, and my 6-hour sprint
excerpt: What happens when the main constraint is not shared? We built an MRT-themed sign language game in 6 hours, and I left with questions about what hackathons are really for.
content:
There is a particular kind of confusion that comes from sprinting at a hackathon, then realising the main constraint is not shared.

Halfway through the Google Gemini 3 Hackathon in Singapore last week, I noticed a "hackathon repo" that clearly did not start that morning.

And I caught myself thinking: is it still a "hackathon" if your repository was initialised three months ago?

On one side, you had teams like mine: starting from scratch, frantically drawing on whiteboards, and hoping nothing weird (quotas, auth, flaky demos) would blindside us.

On the other side, you had teams that seemed to be polishing products they had already been building for days, sometimes weeks.

I later found out one of the winning teams had a company entity established back in October.

Honestly, I genuinely had a great time building with the new Gemini models in a 6-hour sprint.

I did not go with colleagues or random Discord matchups. I kept it close. I partnered with my girlfriend Joey (CS background) and my cousin Cheryl (UI/UX background), and we tried to see what we could pull off in a single day. We were not optimising for the leaderboard. We were optimising for the day.

I realised I miss building things just because they feel interesting, not because they are "strategic", especially after a lot of intense work at a startup the past 6 months.

It is also what I wish organisers were clearer about: whether this is a one-day sprint, or a longer runway showcase.

title: MoSCoW, Velocity, and the Work That Actually Matters
excerpt: MoSCoW taught me how to label priorities. It didn't teach me how to choose.
content:
There's a particular kind of stress that comes from feeling productive every day, yet watching the important thing stay unfinished.

I've felt it most when I'm sitting on a backlog that looks "manageable" in the small: lots of minor bugs, tidy refactors, quick optimisations. The kind of work that gives you clean standup updates and a satisfying "Done" column.

And then there's the other kind of work. The slow, architectural kind. The one that doesn't move in neat increments, but quietly determines whether the next feature launch will be smooth or painful.

This post is about a trap I keep falling into: optimising for visible velocity instead of delivered value.

MoSCoW (Must, Should, Could, Won't) is clean, intuitive, and easy to explain.

The problem is that when you apply it to internal engineering backlogs, it can become a mirror for anxiety instead of a tool for trade-offs.

On paper, "Must" is supposed to mean "we do not ship without this."

In reality, I've watched "Must" absorb everything: a feature needed for a launch, a reliability issue, a demo-prep request from leadership, a piece of tech debt that keeps biting you.

At that point, MoSCoW is still describing something true, but it's no longer helping you decide.

The framing that helped me wasn't "Must vs Should." It was cost of delay: What is the economic cost per week of not having this done?

Frameworks are useful for executing on priorities. They are not a substitute for setting them.

title: The Crossroads of My 20s: What is the One Thing I Cannot Lose?
excerpt: This past year has felt like two lifetimes compressed into twelve months.
content:
This past year has felt like two lifetimes compressed into twelve months, each offering a starkly different vision of what my life could be. As I approach graduation and the final chapter of my undergraduate journey, I feel a mix of excitement and uncertainty as I grapple with the big question of which direction I want to take in life.

The first half of 2024 felt like a dream as I had the privilege to participate in an overseas internship in Paris through my school's NUS Overseas College Program. Living in Paris, I secured my "dream" internship role in a fast-paced startup as an algorithm engineer, working on spatial intelligence solutions. Weekdays were filled with challenging projects and countless opportunities to learn and grow, while weekends were reserved for adventure—traveling across Europe, immersing myself in new cultures, and savoring life's simple pleasures.

It was an experience of balance and freedom. Even during stressful moments at work, the culture prioritized not just productivity but also connection and joy. For the first time in a long while, I felt like I was not just moving through life but truly living it.

The second half of the year, however, brought me back to a different reality. I was consumed by the relentless grind of coursework, learning new technical skills, and applying for internships. Sleep became a luxury, often limited to 3-5 hours a night.

At times, I felt like a sim in a simulation — executing tasks on autopilot, moving from one obligation to the next without truly processing what I was experiencing.

As I stand at this crossroads, I keep returning to one question: what is the one thing I cannot lose? Not the thing I most want to achieve, but the thing whose absence would make everything else feel hollow.

For me, I think the answer is curiosity. The capacity to remain genuinely curious — about work, about people, about the world — feels like the thread I cannot afford to drop.

title: My First Blog Post
excerpt: Hello to everyone reading this! A space for my personal portfolio and life diary.
content:
Hello to everyone reading this! I'm Benedict Chan, currently in my final year of studying Computer Engineering at the National University of Singapore. With graduation around the corner, I figured it was a good time to create a space where I can share more about myself. So here we are - a place for my personal portfolio and maybe even turn it into a bit of a life diary along the way.

I have to admit that this project started off with a very straightforward goal: to pick up some front-end development skills. So far, my work and academic interests have mostly revolved around fields like Computer Vision and Autonomous Robotics. But I figured as a prospective software engineer, it is apt to pick up some basic front-end knowledge. Plus, this gives me a chance to create a personal portfolio—something that feels a bit more "me" compared to LinkedIn.

But as I got deeper into this, I realized I did not want my personal page to just be about my work and projects. I also wanted to showcase the other side of myself that would represent a more "complete" me. Photography has been a long-time passion of mine but I never really had the right place to share my pictures.

Since I'm already building this space, why not go a step further and add a section where I can pen down my random thoughts right? My brain is always on overdrive, and things can get pretty cluttered. By writing it out, I hope to gain some clarity, and maybe even improve my writing in the process.

I'm excited to see where this journey of life takes me as I approach adulthood, and I'd love for you to be part of it!
